extracted.intended_audience: readers and aspiring writers of poetry and prose (particularly those interested in ballads, character-sketches, and classical taste)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and judging narrative/lyric ballads and short character sketches: what makes a ballad feel natural and majestic, and how to render memorable comic or genteel characters through action, language, and small particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and poetical sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentiments in that Ballad are extremely natural and poetical, and full of the majestick Simplicity which we admire in the greatest of the ancient Poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer thoughts and feelings that arise naturally from the subject; let sentiment feel inevitable and sincere rather than contrived. The author stresses 'copyings after Nature' and aligning with the spirit of ancient poets rather than artificial cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epigrammatical turns and points of wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Had this old Song been filled with Epigrammatical Turns and Points of Wit, it might perhaps have pleased the wrong Taste of some Readers; but it would never have become the Delight of the common People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overload a ballad with witty epigrams or clever conceits if the aim is broad, enduring appeal; simplicity and natural emotion better reach both unprejudiced and refined tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majestick language and sonorous numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only the Thought but the Language is majestick, and the Numbers [sonorous]; at least, the Apparel is much more gorgeous than many of the Poets made use of in Queen Elizabeth's Time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dignified diction and sonorous meter where appropriate; rich, resonant phrasing can enhance the poem's grandeur. Balance elevated language with natural sentiment so the poem remains affecting rather than merely ornate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expansive/universal consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: This way of considering the Misfortunes which this Battle would bring upon Posterity ... is wonderfully beautiful, and conformable to the Way of Thinking among the ancient Poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, extend the immediate event to its wider consequences (how it affects future generations or posterity) to achieve a more heroic or epic scope in a narrative ballad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversify catalogues with little characters
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Catalogue of the Slain the Author has followed the Example of the greatest ancient Poets ... not only in giving a long List of the Dead, but by diversifying it with little Characters of particular Persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If including lists or catalogues (e.g., of the dead, of participants), break monotony by inserting brief, distinguishing details or mini-character sketches to humanize and maintain reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid familiar-sounding names when aiming for majesty
rubrics_metrics.description: The familiar Sound in these Names destroys the Majesty of the Description; for this Reason I do not mention this Part of the Poem but to shew the natural Cast of Thought which appears in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of the phonetic and associative qualities of proper names and epithets: overly colloquial or familiar-sounding names can undercut grandeur. Choose names/sounds that sustain the tone you want.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ vivid, natural circumstances in description
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all the descriptive Parts of this Song, there are none more beautiful than the four following Stanzas which have a great Force and Spirit in them, and are filled with very natural Circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete, believable particulars (natural circumstances, small actions) to give force and spirit to descriptions; specifics create verisimilitude and emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of thought within classical spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: The Thought in the third Stanza was never touched by any other Poet, and is such an one as would have shined in Homer or in Virgil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for fresh insights or images even when writing in a classical or traditional mode: originality of thought allied to epic seriousness elevates a poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Gothic/overwrought manner for enduring appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: If this Song had been written in the Gothic Manner, which is the Delight of all our little Wits, whether Writers or Readers, it would not have hit the Taste of so many Ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist overly fanciful, grotesque, or fashion-driven stylistic excesses if you want work to have broad or lasting appeal; classical simplicity often endures better than momentary eccentricity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support critical judgments with authoritative exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall quote several Passages ... not that I would infer ... any Imitation of those Passages, but that he was directed to them in general by the same Kind of Poetical Genius ... I shall only beg Pardon for such a Profusion of Latin Quotations; which I should not have made use of, but that I feared my own Judgment would have looked too singular ... had not I supported it by the Practice and Authority of Virgil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making bold critical claims about taste or quality, buttress them with recognized authorities or illustrative quotations to show the continuity of taste and avoid appearing idiosyncratic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray character via inward principles, not merely outward dress
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cloathing of our Minds certainly ought to be regarded before that of our Bodies. To betray in a Man's Talk a corrupted Imagination, is a much greater Offence against the Conversation of Gentlemen, than any Negligence of Dress imaginable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In character-writing, emphasize moral and intellectual qualities (speech, imagination, temper) over mere external trappings; how a character talks should reveal inner life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine-gentleman character = generosity and bravery
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a Fine Gentleman, is to be a Generous and a Brave Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating a genteel or admirable male character, foreground virtue—generosity and courage—rather than fashion or mannerisms; virtues should inform behavior and presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render rulers and courtiers through social manipulation and small gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: Pharamond ... would by a skilful Cast of his Eye and half a Smile, make two Fellows who hated, embrace and fall upon each other's Neck ... He would, by a skilful Cast of his Eye and half a Smile, make two Fellows ... The Man in Disgrace shall immediately lose all his natural Endowments, and he that finds Favour have the Attributes of an Angel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To depict court life or the effects of favour, show how tiny gestures, looks, and the distribution of favour alter others' behavior and self-regard; use those small social operations to dramatize power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish types of absent-mindedness and show causes
rubrics_metrics.description: I distinguish a Man who is Absent, because he thinks of something else, from one who is Absent, because he thinks of nothing at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing 'absent' or distraite characters, make clear whether absence springs from focused inward thought, passion, or mere vacancy; different causes imply different behaviors and comic or tragic opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete comic misadventures as signals of absent character
rubrics_metrics.description: Menalcas ... opens his Door to go out, but shuts it again, because he perceives that he has his Night-cap on ... he puts his whole Family in an hurry, and at last goes out without being able to stay for his Coach or Dinner ... he swallows down both the Dice, and at the same time throws his Wine into the Tables. He writes a Letter, and flings the Sand into the Ink-bottle; he writes a second, and mistakes the Superscription.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make absent-mindedness vividly comic and believable, populate scenes with absurd, concrete mishaps (wrong coach, misdressed, bungled letters, physical miscues). Specific, repeatable set-pieces create a memorable comic portrait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit others' misperceptions for ironic characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: You would often take him for every thing that he is not; for a Fellow quite stupid, for he hears nothing; for a Fool, for he talks to himself ... The Truth on't is, his Eyes are open, but he makes no use of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the gap between how a character appears to others and what is actually happening inside them to generate irony and deepen characterization; let appearances mislead both characters and readers before revealing reality through specifics.
